# Niloy Biswas

> Niloy Biswas is an AI/LLM engineer and data analyst at 10 Minute School in Dhaka, Bangladesh. He works on TenTen, 10MS's AI study partner (RAG, intent routing, product analytics), and on BigQuery and Data Studio data systems. His machine-learning research is published in Hindawi's BioMed Research International.

Based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Open to remote roles and projects. Site: https://niloy.tech

## TenTen: AI Study Partner

URL: https://niloy.tech/projects/tenten/

← Back to Case Studies & Projects

Hello, I'm

TenTen

TenTen - Bangladesh's First Integrated

AI Learning Ecosystem

A 10-month journey building TenTen, the AI study partner inside the 10 Minute School app: from early R&D in Google Colab to production RAG, Bangla LLM behaviour, intent routing, and product analytics after a limited release in Nov '25.

Product area

AI study partner (TenTen)

My role

AI/LLM Engineer & Data Analyst

Platform

10 Minute School app

Timeline

~10 months R&D · Nov '25 launch

View product

The problem

When learning paused, students had nowhere to turn

10 Minute School reaches millions of learners across Bangladesh, many of them without access to private tutoring. Students on the platform could learn, but they had no way to recover when they got confused.

Four issues kept showing up:

Stuck watching a recorded class. No teacher available to ask for clarification.

Stuck after reading an exam explanation that still didn't make sense. Stuck with no one to ask.

Stuck on a theory question with nowhere useful to look for a real explanation.

Stuck during live class, with doubts piling up and platform help buried in FAQ pages nobody reads.

That meant the product was good at delivering content but had no answer for the moment after confusion. And in education, that moment matters more than almost anything else. It is where students pause, skip, guess, or quietly give up.

Before TenTen, support meant FAQ pages and external chatbots with zero curriculum context. Learning broke at the exact moments students needed help most, and nothing inside 10MS could stitch it back together.

The solution

Not a regular chatbot

Solving academic challenges inside the learning journey

TenTen lives exactly where learning breaks: inside general chat, recorded lessons, exam review, and live class. It is built into 10 Minute School, not bolted on as a separate chat window, so help arrives with the student's class, grade, and curriculum context already in place.

Solve problems on demand

Study partner, not teacher. TenTen does not lecture. It helps students work through confusion the way a smart classmate would: step by step, in Bangla when they need it.

Ground answers in what they're learning

Academic doubts pull from textbooks and trusted 10MS content. Platform questions route elsewhere. Students get the right kind of help instead of one generic reply for every intent.

Grow alongside the learner

As students use TenTen across surfaces, it stays aware of their progress: what they watched, what they got wrong, what to revise next. Guidance deepens instead of resetting every session.

With TenTen, the product finally supports the moment after confusion, not just content consumption. A study partner embedded in the learning journey, not another chatbot students have to leave the app to find.

What I built

Four systems shipped across a ten-month build: retrieval, routing, orchestration, and analytics.

From pilot to product

Where the engineering work fit in TenTen's story

The work covered the data and AI layer: retrieval, routing, and orchestration that turned early Colab, n8n, and Dify experiments into production systems the product could actually trust.

Eight phases from research through limited release. The cards below are the four pillars that shipped across that arc.

R&D

Prototype to production orchestration

~10 months of retrieval and prompt experiments in Colab, n8n, and Dify before production wiring.

Migrated orchestration to LangGraph for agent flows, state, and production control.

Colab n8n Dify LangGraph

RAG

Curriculum-grounded retrieval

Evidence from textbooks and trusted 10MS content, with eval loops on retrieval quality.

Semantic chunking , hybrid search (semantic + keyword), and reranking before generation.

Semantic chunking Hybrid search Reranking

Routing

Mixed-intent handling

Separate paths for academic doubts vs platform and logistics questions.

Academic and general agents , a 10MS MCP server , and subject-wise user memory retrieved when needed.

Multi-agent MCP User memory

Analytics

Post-launch measurement

Data-led iteration after limited release in Nov '25.

Usage, retention, session depth, and answer helpfulness fed back into product and model improvements.

Usage Retention Helpfulness

Engineering challenges

Why those systems were necessary: the constraints and failure modes that shaped every decision, not just an implementation checklist.

অ

Bangla in the wild

Students rarely write textbook Bangla. Code-mixed shorthand, typos, and spoken phrasing break assumptions baked into base models and clean training data.

A fluent-sounding wrong answer erodes trust faster than an honest "I'm not sure."

?

Sparse questions, dense books

A six-word doubt has to land in the right NCTB paragraph inside a long chapter. Vector similarity alone often returns plausible-but-wrong passages.

Retrieval mistakes look like knowledge mistakes to a student who can't verify the source.

◎

One chat, many jobs

The same input handles physics steps, class timing, pricing, and platform help. Routing errors send academic answers to logistics questions, or flip it the other way around.

Wrong intent is worse than no answer when students are already stuck.

How TenTen shows up for students

Four learning surfaces, one integrated study partner across the moments that matter most. Not four separate chatbots.

General chat

24/7 doubt solving

Ask any academic question, anytime. Step-by-step help across every subject.

Live class

Doubts during and after class

Learning support inside live sessions. Ask a question without breaking the flow.

Recorded class

Help without leaving the video

Ask about a specific moment in a recorded lesson. Context travels with the question.

Exam solution

Understand why an answer was wrong

Instant explanations after exams. Follow up on any MCQ you got wrong and actually understand why.

Numbers that came back stronger than expected after just months of rollout.

What this means

More than a tool. Part of how a generation learns.

Solving the basics is only the starting point. As the largest edTech platform in Bangladesh, there is a responsibility to bring bold innovations that actually reshape how students learn. That means reaching every division, from rural classrooms to city prep centers, with AI that grows alongside how students study.

## USAID HSEP: Teacher Training Analytics

URL: https://niloy.tech/projects/hsep/

← Back to Case Studies & Projects

Learning analytics case study · USAID HSEP · Bangladesh

Measuring USAID's teacher training pilot in Bangladesh until the aid freeze stopped it

In late 2024, 479 college teachers and education leaders from 57 districts took the first online cohort of USAID's Higher Secondary Education Project (HSEP, also referred to as HSEA) in Bangladesh. I led the data side on the 10 Minute School team. The pilot's last module closed on January 19, 2025. Five days later a US stop-work order froze foreign aid, and the next cohort never started.

HSEP's annual work-planning workshop in Dhaka, with partners, trainers and education officials.

479

Pilot participants (382 TPD, 97 ELPD)

111,693

Learning events logged during the pilot

407

Colleges and institutes represented

Jan 24

2025 stop-work order on US foreign aid

The program

A five-year, $40M plan to retrain Bangladesh's college teachers

Higher secondary education (grades 11 and 12) is often overlooked by international donors . HSEP, officially "USAID's Higher Secondary Education Activity", was the exception: a five-year program implemented by Chemonics International under Bangladesh's Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE). Florida State University certified the training, and 10 Minute School held a $2.93M subaward to deploy and customize the learning management system (LMS) it ran on.

$40M

USAID plan, Aug 2023 to Aug 2028

12,000

Trainees targeted by Sept 2025

~60,000

Trainees targeted by Aug 2028

Nov 10

2024 pilot launch in Bogura

About 500 participants started in person at three venues (Bogura, Cumilla and Khulna), then moved online into two programs: TPD (Teachers Professional Development, 8 modules) and ELPD (Educational Leadership Professional Development, 7 modules). Going from 479 people to 12,000 in under a year meant every pilot decision would be copied about 25 times. The pilot data had to show which decisions were worth copying.

A face-to-face session during the HSEP program. The online modules picked up where these sessions ended.

My role and the team

Where the data work sat

I was a Senior BI Analyst at 10 Minute School and the data lead on HSEP. Shazzad Hossain Mukit and Shihab managed the product. Shad Iqbal led design, with product designers Moshiur Hridoy and Diponkar shaping the learning flows, peer review and discussion features. Moshiur has written up the design story, including the 21-day prototype sprint and field testing with teachers, in his own HSEP case study . This page is the other half: what the platform data said.

Modeled the LMS data in BigQuery and set the filter that kept only real pilot participants

Defined the activation, completion and peer review metrics, and built the Data Studio (formerly Looker Studio) dashboard all four partner organizations used

Built the data pipeline and scoring behind the 36-item pre-training diagnostic run at the three training sites

Re-ran every number on this page against the raw tables before publishing it

The measurement problem

Four partners, four definitions of a good pilot

Each organization opened the dashboard with a different question. If each one had picked its own favorite number, the pilot would have looked like four different projects. So the dashboard kept every metric on the same footing (enrolled teachers as the denominator, filters for batch, program, module and day) and let each partner start from the view that answered them.

What each partner needed from the pilot data

Partner

Their question

Where the dashboard answered it

USAID

Is the money reaching teachers in a way that can scale?

Enrollment and activation by batch and district

Florida State University

Are teachers learning what the curriculum teaches?

Exam attempts and scores, the pre-training diagnostic

Chemonics International

Is the rollout on schedule?

Completion by each module's end date, peer review throughput

DSHE (Ministry of Education)

Are college teachers taking it up?

Activity by district and institution type, learning time

The data model

One row for every teacher and every piece of content

The LMS wrote to several services: reading and video logs, exam sessions, peer review, and the live-class schedule. Those synced into BigQuery, and the reporting model joined them into a grid with one row for each enrolled teacher and each content item in their batch, 109,180 rows in all. An empty timestamp means the teacher never opened that item. That made "who hasn't started Module 3" as easy to ask as "who finished it", which a plain event log can't answer without extra work.

LMS services Logs, exams, peer review, live classes

BigQuery Raw tables from each service

Teacher x content model Real participants only, matched to the official pilot list

Data Studio Filters for batch, program, module and day

Activated: opened at least one content item from that module-day.

Completed: finished 80% or more of that module-day's content.

Both rates divide by enrolled teachers, so a teacher who goes quiet pulls the rate down instead of dropping out of it.

Timestamps are stored in UTC. Anything about time of day is converted to Bangladesh time (UTC+6) first.

What the data showed

Teachers kept showing up. They finished a little less as each module went on

Every TPD module runs five days. Averaged over all 8 modules, the share of teachers who opened something each day never fell below 92.7%. Completion at the 80% bar started at 94.2% on Day 1 and ended at 77.9% on Day 5. Day 4 is the exception in the chart: it holds a single task or live session, so anyone who opened it also completed it.

The same slow slide shows up across modules. In TPD, completion went from 93% in Module 1 to 84% in Module 8. Counting only work finished before each module's deadline, 70% to 82% of TPD teachers completed on time.

Activation (opened at least one item)

Completion (80% or more of the day)

Peer review held up at one reviewer and strained at two

Submitting work was never the weak point: 95% of TPD teachers handed in at least one task, and 84% were still submitting in Module 8. The strain was on the reviewing side. Every submission went to classmates for review, and each task set a minimum. Where one review was enough, 92% of submissions got it. Where the task asked for two, only 55% reached the bar, even though 89% got at least one. The second reviewer was the one who often never came.

Tasks needing 1 review (2,051 TPD submissions)

92%

Tasks needing 2 reviews (647 TPD submissions)

Gap

55%

Share of submissions that reached the task's review minimum, from the peer review service's own task settings.

Who finished, and when they studied

Teachers studied after college hours. Activity was heaviest between 6 PM and 11 PM Bangladesh time and peaked at 8 PM. The typical TPD teacher logged about 10.5 hours of reading and video, and that excludes time spent in exams and live classes, which the logs don't record. In exams, TPD teachers made 8,778 attempts across 13 exams, about 1.9 tries per exam, and averaged 77%. ELPD averaged 84%.

Completion also varied by type of institution. Women were only 51 of the 479 teachers, but their module completion rate matched the men's at 88%.

MPO colleges (105 teachers)

95%

Government colleges (268)

89%

Non-MPO colleges (58)

83%

Higher Secondary Teachers' Training Institutes (31)

77%

Module completion rate (80% bar) by institution type. MPO colleges are non-government colleges that receive government salary support.

The pre-training diagnostic pointed at two beliefs

Before the online modules, teachers at all three training sites answered a 36-item diagnostic on Knowledge, Skills and Attitudes. Knowledge was the weakest area at 68% to 71% correct, against 79% to 86% for the other two. The lowest items clustered around two ideas: that action research is only about end-of-term grading, and that every student should get the same instruction regardless of age, gender or ability. Changing that second belief was the point of the differentiated-instruction content.

"Action research involves only summative assessment" (should disagree)

Below 50%

30%

"Same instruction regardless of age, gender, or ability" (should disagree)

Below 50%

37%

"Instruction should stay the same for all students" (should disagree)

Below 50%

39%

"Engaged Learning Pedagogy can't work online" (should disagree)

60%

"Engaged learning only works in small classes" (should disagree)

74%

Average share answering correctly across Cumilla, Khulna and Bogura. Items under 50% were flagged as priorities for the next training phase.

The shutdown

The pilot finished. The next cohort never started

The pilot launched five days after the 2024 US presidential election, and its last module closed the day before the new administration took office. What followed moved fast.

Nov 10, 2024 Pilot launches in Bogura, with Cumilla and Khulna linked in.

Nov 17, 2024 First online module unlocks on the platform.

Jan 19, 2025 Last pilot module closes.

Jan 20, 2025 An executive order pauses new US foreign aid spending for a 90-day review.

Jan 24, 2025 The State Department issues a stop-work order on existing aid grants and contracts.

Jan 26, 2025 USAID tells all its partners in Bangladesh to suspend spending until further notice.

Feb 2025 Three pilot teachers log 10 events between them, all month.

Mar 10, 2025 The Secretary of State announces that 83% of USAID programs are cancelled.

Jul 1, 2025 USAID closes and the State Department takes over foreign assistance.

Reuters, January 25, 2025.

The edge in the data is clean. 99% of all pilot activity happened on or before January 25. Teachers doing graded work (exam attempts or task submissions) went from more than 420 a month to none.

Teachers doing graded work each month

Nov '24

461

Dec '24

466

Jan '25

422

Feb '25

0

Out of 479 pilot teachers. Pilot modules ran Nov 17 to Jan 19. Stop-work order: January 24, 2025.

Reaching 12,000 trainees by September 2025 depended on the cohorts that were supposed to follow the pilot, and none of them launched. HSEP was not alone. The Daily Star reported that 55 of the 59 USAID projects in Bangladesh were shut down , costing the country about $700M in aid. Public records don't list a termination date for HSEP itself. The logs show the work stopped when the stop-work order arrived.

What I took from it

Lessons I still use

Pick the denominator before anyone sees a chart. Dividing every rate by enrolled teachers made the dashboard hard to flatter, and it meant four organizations with different goals were reading the same number.

Measure against what the system asked for. The design notes imagined three peer reviewers per submission. The platform asked for one or two. Which bar you pick decides whether peer review looks like it worked.

The dataset outlives the program. When funding stopped overnight, the BigQuery tables were what remained. Every number here was re-run from them more than a year and a half later.

Sources

Award and subaward records: USAspending.gov, cooperative agreement 72038823CA00007

Program scope: Chemonics project page (archived December 2024)

Program targets and pilot launch: New Age, November 10, 2024

Bangladesh project shutdowns: The Daily Star, May 2025

Platform metrics: HSEP BigQuery project, re-queried October 2026. Raw data is not public because it contains participant information.

## Chicago Taxi Trips

URL: https://niloy.tech/projects/chicago-taxi/

This Data Studio (formerly Looker Studio) dashboard explores the City of Chicago's public taxi dataset in BigQuery for January 2015 to March 2023: 142.0M trips, 9.2K taxis and $2.4B in revenue. Yearly trips fall from 32.4M in 2015 to 3.9M in 2020 and 2021, with a partial rebound to 6.4M in 2022, while demand stays concentrated downtown and along the lakefront.

Google BigQuery

SQL

Data Studio

View live dashboard in Data Studio

Key facts

Purpose Personal exploration of an open dataset

Data source Public BigQuery table bigquery-public-data.chicago_taxi_trips.taxi_trips , from the City of Chicago's "Taxi Trips (2013-2023)" dataset

Dashboard window January 1, 2015 to March 31, 2023

Scale on the dashboard 142.0M trips, 867.9M km, 9.2K taxis, $2.4B revenue

Filters Date range, payment method, company

Stack BigQuery (custom SQL), Data Studio

Output Two-page Data Studio report (linked above)

The question

This started as an exploration of the City of Chicago's open taxi dataset in BigQuery. The question that shaped the dashboard: how has Chicago's taxi market changed between 2015 and 2023, and where do trips and revenue concentrate? Each chart answers one part of it: market size, payment habits, trip length, company share and geography.

Data and approach

The City of Chicago publishes taxi trips reported to it as a regulatory agency. Each row is one trip, with start and end times, seconds and miles travelled, pickup and dropoff locations, fare, tips, tolls, extras, total, payment type and company. The BigQuery copy holds 213,111,447 rows, about 83 GB, from January 2013 to December 2023 (counted on October 10, 2026).

That is a lot of data for an interactive report, so I limited the window to 2015 onward to keep the volume manageable. The dashboard reads from a custom SQL query in BigQuery connected to Data Studio. Page one has KPI tiles for trips, km travelled, taxis, revenue and revenue per km, filters for date, payment method and company, four yearly charts and a company table. Page two has a company revenue race, pickup and dropoff heatmaps and a table of individual taxis.

What the data shows

A market that shrank before 2020

In 2015 there were 7.8K taxis on the road and 32.4M trips, and 2016 was close behind with 8K taxis and 31.8M trips. Then trips fell every year: 25M in 2017, 20.7M in 2018 and 16.5M in 2019, when 5.6K taxis were running. That is about half the 2015 volume before 2020 began.

In 2020 trips dropped to 3.9M and stayed at 3.9M in 2021, with taxis at 2.6K. 2022 recovered partly, to 6.4M trips and 3K taxis. The 2023 bar of 1.4M trips and 2.7K taxis covers January to March only, because of the date filter, so it is not a further collapse.

Payments moved from cash to cards

Cash is the largest slice of the payment mix in 2015, at roughly 57%, and it shrinks every year to about 31% in 2023. Credit card takes most of the difference and is the biggest share by 2023. Mobile payments are a thin sliver in 2019 and 2020 and by 2022 and 2023 make up roughly a sixth of the mix.

Fewer rides, but longer ones

Average trip duration rises from 12.4 minutes in 2015 to 15 in 2019, then to 19.1 in 2021, 20 in 2022 and 19 in 2023. Average speed was 24.5 km/h in 2015 and 20.1 in 2019, then 33.3 in 2021 and 33.8 in 2022. Since trips after 2020 are both longer in time and faster, the average ride covers more distance than in 2015. Revenue per km fell from $8.12 in 2015 to $5.84 in 2017 and climbed to $9.82 in 2022.

Revenue sits with a few companies

Among the top rows of the company table, Taxi Affiliation Services leads on trips and revenue: 2,649 taxis, 25.5M trips (about 18% of the 142.0M) and $420.08M. Flash Cab follows with 1,575 taxis, 16.9M trips and $297.5M. Chicago Carriage Cab Corp ($139.63M), Yellow Cab ($125.3M), Sun Taxi ($123.7M) and City Service ($117.66M) sit in a band between $117M and $140M. In the January 2022 frame of the revenue race on page two, Taxi Affiliation Services has the longest bar, followed by Flash Cab and Chicago Carriage Cab Corp.

Trips cluster downtown and on the lakefront

The pickup and dropoff heatmaps look alike. Both peak downtown and along the lakefront strip to the north, and the scales top out at 20.1M pickups and 17.3M dropoffs. A second, separate hotspot sits to the northwest around O'Hare International Airport, next to Rosemont, and it is stronger for pickups than for dropoffs. Smaller patches appear south-west of downtown, and the suburbs show little activity.

Data caveats

One company group is null, with 2,175 taxis, 13.2M trips and $202.92M, about 9% of the 142.0M trips.

Suburban Dispatch LLC shows an average trip duration of 0.21 minutes and an average revenue per km of 569,830.77, which the table highlights as an outlier.

The City says not all trips are reported, though it believes most are. Times are rounded to 15 minutes, some census tracts are suppressed for privacy, and cash tips are generally not recorded.

Questions

How many taxi trips are there in Chicago per year?

In the dashboard, trips run from 32.4M in 2015 and 31.8M in 2016 down to 25M in 2017, 20.7M in 2018 and 16.5M in 2019. They were 3.9M in both 2020 and 2021 and 6.4M in 2022. The 1.4M shown for 2023 is January to March only.

How did COVID-19 affect Chicago taxi trips?

Trips fell from 16.5M in 2019 to 3.9M in 2020, a drop of about three quarters, and stayed at 3.9M in 2021 before reaching 6.4M in 2022. Taxis on the road went from 5.6K in 2019 to 4.5K in 2020 and 2.6K in 2021. Trips had already been falling since 2015, so 2020 is a steep drop on top of a long decline.

Which taxi company earns the most in Chicago?

For January 2015 to March 2023, Taxi Affiliation Services leads the dashboard's company table with $420.08M from 25.5M trips, ahead of Flash Cab at $297.5M from 16.9M trips. Trips with no company recorded add another $202.92M that cannot be assigned to a company.

---

## Heart Disease Prediction

URL: https://niloy.tech/projects/heart-disease/

This published study (BioMed Research International, 2023) tested six machine learning models for early heart disease prediction on 303 patient records from the UCI Cleveland dataset. It has ten authors, and Niloy Biswas is the first. A support vector machine on nine selected features scored best at 94.51% accuracy, and logistic regression followed at 93.41%.

Python

Matplotlib

Scikit-learn

View the code on GitHub

Read the published paper

ROC curves of the six models on the nine-feature subset (SF3), with AUC values in the legend.

Key facts

Paper "Machine Learning-Based Model to Predict Heart Disease in Early Stage Employing Different Feature Selection Techniques," BioMed Research International, 2023, article 6864343, doi:10.1155/2023/6864343 (published May 2, 2023, open access, CC BY)

Authors Niloy Biswas (first author) and nine co-authors from Daffodil International University, Charles Darwin University, MBSTU, University of Saskatchewan, Umm Al-Qura University and the University of Queensland

My role I ran the core experiments, validated the results, created the charts and wrote the methodology and results sections. Co-authors Kawsar Ahmed and Mohammad Ali Moni provided the idea and designed the experiments, and the team analyzed the data and wrote the manuscript together.

Dataset UCI Cleveland heart disease data: 303 patient records, 13 features, binary target (disease or no disease)

Split 70% training, 30% test (91 test records)

Feature selection ANOVA F value, chi-square and mutual information

Models Logistic regression, decision tree, random forest, support vector machine (RBF kernel), Gaussian naive Bayes and K-nearest neighbors

Best result Support vector machine on nine features: 94.51% accuracy, 94.87% sensitivity, 94.23% specificity, AUROC 94.95, log loss 0.31

Stack Python 3.8, Pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, Matplotlib, seaborn, Jupyter; code on GitHub

The problem

Cardiovascular disease causes about 17.9 million deaths a year, 32% of all deaths worldwide according to the WHO. Finding it early lowers mortality, so the paper asks which machine learning model, and which clinical features, can flag heart disease reliably at an early stage.

Data

The dataset is the UCI Cleveland heart disease data: 303 patient records with 13 features and a binary target. The features are age, sex, chest pain type ( cp ), resting blood pressure ( trestbps ), cholesterol ( chol ), fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dl ( fbs ), resting ECG ( restecg ), maximum heart rate ( thalach ), exercise-induced angina ( exang ), ST depression ( oldpeak ), the slope of the peak exercise ST segment, the number of major vessels colored by fluoroscopy ( ca ) and the thallium stress test result ( thal ).

Approach

Preprocessing replaced four incorrect values in ca and two in thal , then scaled every feature with StandardScaler to mean 0 and variance 1. The data was split 70/30 into training and test sets.

Three feature selection methods ranked the 13 features. ANOVA put exang (70.95), cp (69.77) and oldpeak (68.55) on top. Chi-square ranked thalach (188.32), oldpeak (72.64) and ca (70.89) highest. Mutual information favored cp (0.17), thal (0.14) and ca (0.11).

From these rankings the team built three feature subsets: SF1 with all 13 features, SF2 with 10 features (dropping trestbps , fbs and restecg ), and SF3 with nine features (age, sex, cp , thalach , exang , oldpeak , slope, ca and thal ). Each of the six models was trained and tested on every subset, and scored on accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, AUROC and log loss.

Study workflow. Figure 1 from Biswas et al. (2023) , BioMed Research International, CC BY 4.0.

Results

Test accuracy in percent on the 91 held-out records.

Test accuracy by model and feature subset

Model SF1 (13 features) SF2 (10 features) SF3 (9 features)

Logistic regression 93.41 93.41 93.41

Support vector machine 90.11 89.01 94.51

Gaussian naive Bayes 89.01 90.11 90.11

Random forest 87.91 86.81 84.61

K-nearest neighbors 83.52 92.31 91.21

Decision tree 78.02 76.92 75.82

The support vector machine on SF3 was the best single result: 94.51% accuracy, 94.87% sensitivity, 94.23% specificity, AUROC 94.95 and log loss 0.31. Logistic regression was the steadiest model, at 93.41% on all three subsets. It had the best AUROC (96.08, on SF3) and the lowest log loss (0.27, on SF2 and SF3). The paper concludes that the support vector machine and logistic regression performed best, and argues the approach could support early, low-cost heart disease prediction in clinical settings.

The decision tree was the weakest model, with accuracy of 75.82 to 78.02 and log loss between 7.59 and 8.35. The ROC figure above shows the nine-feature subset: logistic regression 0.961, Gaussian naive Bayes 0.955, support vector machine 0.950, random forest 0.939, K-nearest neighbors 0.938 and decision tree 0.795.

The abstract labels the 94.51% model as random forest; the results section, ROC curves and comparison table identify it as the support vector machine, which also matches the repository code.

What the features say

Chest pain type, exercise-induced angina, ST depression, maximum heart rate, the number of colored vessels and the thallium result carry the most signal. Each ranks near the top under at least one of the three methods. Fasting blood sugar, resting ECG, resting blood pressure and cholesterol score low under all three, which is why the smaller subsets drop them.

Dropping them did not hurt the best models. Logistic regression stayed at 93.41% on all three subsets, and the support vector machine and K-nearest neighbors reached their best accuracy on the smaller ones. In this dataset, disease cases also concentrate in middle age, roughly 41 to 54.

The paper’s correlation heat map shows the same split. Almost all features are only weakly correlated with each other, so few of them are redundant enough to remove. Against the target, chest pain type, maximum heart rate and slope correlate most positively, exercise-induced angina, ST depression and the number of colored vessels most negatively, and fasting blood sugar, cholesterol, resting blood pressure and resting ECG the least.

Correlation between the 13 features and the target, clustered. Figure 4 from Biswas et al. (2023) , BioMed Research International, CC BY 4.0.

Limitations

The dataset is small, with 303 records and a 91-record test set, so the results should be tested on larger real-world patient data. The authors name deep learning as future work. The data is available from the corresponding author on request, and the notebooks behind the experiments are in the GitHub repository .

Questions

Which machine learning model is best for heart disease prediction?

In this study, a support vector machine on nine selected features was best, at 94.51% accuracy. Logistic regression came close at 93.41% and held that score on all three feature subsets. The decision tree was the weakest at 75.82 to 78.02%.

Which features matter most for predicting heart disease?

Chest pain type, exercise-induced angina, ST depression, maximum heart rate, the number of colored vessels and the thallium stress result ranked highest across ANOVA, chi-square and mutual information. Fasting blood sugar, resting ECG, resting blood pressure and cholesterol scored low under all three.

What dataset is used for heart disease prediction with machine learning?

The study uses the UCI Cleveland heart disease dataset: 303 patient records, 13 clinical features and a binary target for disease or no disease.

## BigQuery Cost Monitoring

URL: https://niloy.tech/projects/bigquery-cost-monitoring/

The 10 Minute School data team's BigQuery spend had grown to the point where we needed to see which query, dashboard or connector was responsible. This project reads region-us.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS , estimates the cost of every job and attributes it to the person, the Connected Sheets connector or the Data Studio (formerly Looker Studio) report behind it. The whole data team reviews the dashboard every week and optimizes queries when something stands out.

Data Analytics

Google BigQuery

Data Studio

SQL

GCP

Read the step-by-step guide on Medium

Key facts

Context 10 Minute School data team

Data source region-us.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS , BigQuery's job metadata view

Attribution User, requestor or Connected Sheets connector label, Data Studio report, destination and referenced tables

Cost basis total_bytes_billed at $6.25 per TiB on-demand, an estimate and not an invoice line

Review cadence Weekly, by the whole data team

Stack BigQuery SQL, Data Studio

The problem

On-demand BigQuery bills each query job for the bytes it processes, so a month of spend is the sum of thousands of small jobs. The bill shows totals by project and SKU. It does not say who ran a job, which report triggered it or which table it read. As our spend grew, the team needed exactly that: which query, which Data Studio report or which connector is responsible for the cost.

The query

INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS holds running jobs plus job history for the past 180 days. It is queried one region at a time, and its data is partitioned by creation_time , so filtering on that column limits what the query scans. The query below returns one row per job.

SELECT

JOBS.project_id,

user_email,

SPLIT(user_email, '@')[OFFSET(0)] Name,

job_id,

destination_table.dataset_id as destination_table_dataset_id,

destination_table.table_id as destination_table_table_id,

COALESCE((SELECT value FROM UNNEST(labels) WHERE key = 'requestor'), (SELECT value FROM UNNEST(labels) WHERE key = 'sheets_connector')) AS requestor,

CONCAT("https://lookerstudio.google.com/u/0/reporting/", (SELECT value FROM UNNEST(labels) WHERE key = 'looker_studio_report_id')) Dashboard_Link,

referenced_tables[SAFE_OFFSET(0)].dataset_id AS referenced_tables_dataset_id,

referenced_tables[SAFE_OFFSET(0)].table_id AS referenced_tables_table_id,

DateTime(creation_time) Date_Time,

FORMAT_TIMESTAMP('%Y-%m-%d %I:%M %p', TIMESTAMP_ADD(creation_time, INTERVAL 6 HOUR)) AS dhaka_time,

job_type,

statement_type,

priority,

query,

state,

(total_bytes_processed / (1024 * 1024 * 1024)) Byte_Processed_GB,

total_bytes_billed,

total_bytes_billed / (1024 * 1024 * 1024) AS total_GB_billed,

(total_bytes_billed / (1024 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024)) * 6.25 AS Cost_USD

FROM region-us.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS

WHERE

Date(creation_time) >=

DATE(FORMAT_DATE('%Y-%m-01', CURRENT_DATE() - 31)) -- Previous months starting

ORDER BY creation_time DESC

The columns group by the question they answer:

Who. user_email , a short Name taken from before the @ , and requestor , which reads the job's requestor label and falls back to the sheets_connector label for Connected Sheets.

Which report. Dashboard_Link turns the looker_studio_report_id label into a clickable link to the Data Studio report that issued the job.

Which tables. destination_table_* is where results were written. referenced_tables_* is the first source table the job read.

When. Date_Time is UTC. dhaka_time adds 6 hours for Dhaka local time.

What kind of job. job_type , statement_type , priority , state and the query text.

How much. Byte_Processed_GB and total_GB_billed divide by 1024 3 , so they are GiB despite the column names. Cost_USD divides billed bytes by 1024 4 to get TiB and multiplies by 6.25.

The WHERE clause keeps a rolling window that starts on the first day of the previous month, so the dashboard always has last month to compare against.

What changed from the first version

The original query is in the 2023 Medium post . It showed who ran a job and what it cost. This version was rewritten for more granular attribution:

Job labels attribute cost to the requester and to the exact Data Studio report, instead of only to a user account.

referenced_tables shows which source table a job read.

Dhaka time sits next to UTC, so hourly patterns read in local time.

Units are binary (GiB and TiB) and the rate is the current $6.25 per TiB on-demand, replacing the old flat $5 per decimal TB.

The window is rolling instead of a hard-coded start date.

Two practical notes if you adapt it. The estimate is gross: it does not subtract the free first 1 TiB per month, and it leaves out storage cost. If your workload uses scripts, add AND statement_type != 'SCRIPT' to the WHERE clause, because a script row includes summary values for its child jobs and summing both counts them twice.

The dashboard

The query is pasted as a custom query on the SQL tab of a BigQuery data source in Data Studio, and one dashboard sits on top of it. As the screenshot shows, it has a total cost scorecard with date and name filters, then:

Cost over time. Daily cost as a line over bars of job counts, to spot trends and spikes.

Cost by person. Total jobs, cost and average cost per job for each account, to find outliers.

Cost by hour. Jobs and cost across the day, to see when usage peaks.

Cost per job by date. A pivot of jobs, GB billed and cost for each person and day.

Detailed query table. Individual jobs sorted by cost, with the user, priority, query text and destination.

How the team uses it

Reviewing the dashboard is a weekly habit for the whole data team. We look for the jobs at the top of the cost table, check who or what issued them, and follow the Dashboard_Link when a Data Studio report is the source. When a query or a report is scanning more than it needs to, we optimize it.

Questions

How do I see which Data Studio report is driving BigQuery cost?

Jobs started by Data Studio carry a looker_studio_report_id label. Read it from the labels column of INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS and append it to https://lookerstudio.google.com/u/0/reporting/ , as the query above does, to get a link to the report. Sum the cost by that link to rank reports.

How do you calculate BigQuery query cost from INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS?

Divide total_bytes_billed by 1024 4 to get TiB and multiply by your on-demand rate. Google's pricing page, checked in October 2026, lists $6.25 per TiB for Iowa (us-central1), and rates vary by region. total_bytes_billed is only meaningful for projects on on-demand pricing. For flat-rate projects Google documents it as informational.

Does INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS cost include the free tier?

No. The first 1 TiB of query processing each month is free on on-demand pricing, but the query multiplies every billed byte by the rate. Subtract the free tier from the monthly total if you want a figure closer to the invoice.

Dhaka - As the bustling capital of Bangladesh, with a population of more than 44 million people, the city exudes life. Immerse yourself in the complexities of this densely populated metropolis, where each district tells a unique tale due to the sheer density of its residents.

## CRM Sales Performance Dashboard

URL: https://niloy.tech/projects/crm-sales/

This Data Studio (formerly Looker Studio) dashboard was the live-dashboard project in the Data Analytics Bootcamp at Human Development Network Bangladesh (HDNB), used to teach students how to build a live dashboard from CRM sales data. It shows 10.0M in total sales, an average sales value of 1.5K and 48 average days to close. It splits the results by month, product, sector and sales manager, and compares the six managers on sales, win rate and time to close.

Google BigQuery

SQL

Google Sheets

Data Studio

View live dashboard in Data Studio

Key facts

Context Teaching project, Data Analytics Bootcamp at HDNB (2024)

Dataset Sample CRM sales opportunities for six sales managers, with products, sectors and deal stages

Time window Monthly view from March to December 2017, plus a bucket of orders with no month

Scale 10.0M total sales and 8,800 orders in the manager table, of which 4,238 are won

Filters Product, date range, sector, manager

Stack BigQuery, SQL, Google Sheets and Data Studio

Why it was built

From May to August 2024 I taught SQL in the Data Analytics Bootcamp run by HDNB, from database basics through window functions and query tuning, ending with how to create and manage live dashboards. This dashboard was the course project for that last part: students used it to learn how CRM opportunity records turn into scorecards, trends, mix charts and a manager comparison that update as the data changes.

The data is a sample CRM dataset used for teaching, so the figures below show what the dashboard surfaces, not a real company's results.

What the dashboard contains

Three scorecards (total sales, average sales value, average days to close) sit above a monthly chart of sales against orders. Two pie charts show the product and sector mix. A manager section has two stacked bar charts, one by product family (GTX, MG, GTK) and one by deal stage, and a table with sales, average order value (AOV), average days to close, total orders, orders won and win rate for each manager.

What the dashboard shows

Monthly sales and orders. Monthly sales run from 696.9K in July to 1.3M in June, and monthly orders from 566 in October to 805 in May. The two do not move together: June has the highest sales on 641 orders, while May has the most orders and 1M in sales. A further 2.1K orders sit in a "null" month bucket.

Product mix. GTXPro has the largest share at 35.1%, then GTX Plus Pro at 26.3% and MG Advanced at 22.2%. GTX Plus Basic, GTX Basic and GTK 500 are 7%, 5% and 4%.

Sector mix. Retail is largest at 18.7%, then technology at 15.1% and medical at 13.6%. Software, finance and marketing are each between 9.2% and 10.8%.

Managers. Across the six managers, 4,238 of 8,800 orders are won, which is 48.2%. The table below shows the spread.

Manager performance table (names are from the sample dataset)

Manager Sales AOV Avg. days to close Orders Won Win rate

Melvin Marxen 2,251,930 1,588 47.8 1,929 882 45.72%

Summer Sewald 1,964,750 1,527 48.5 1,701 828 48.68%

Rocco Neubert 1,960,545 1,761 45.8 1,327 691 52.07%

Celia Rouche 1,603,897 1,667 47.5 1,296 610 47.07%

Cara Losch 1,130,049 1,517 49.0 964 480 49.79%

Dustin Brinkmann 1,094,363 923 49.4 1,583 747 47.19%

Melvin Marxen has the highest sales and the lowest win rate of the six. Rocco Neubert has the highest win rate (52.07%), the highest AOV (1,761) and the fastest average close (45.8 days). Dustin Brinkmann has the lowest AOV (923) on 1,583 orders. The manager sales add up to 10,005,534, matching the 10.0M scorecard.

Questions

Which sales manager has the highest win rate in the CRM dashboard?

Rocco Neubert, at 52.07% (691 of 1,327 orders), followed by Cara Losch at 49.79%. The highest total sales belong to Melvin Marxen at 2,251,930, whose win rate of 45.72% is the lowest of the six.

What is the average days to close in this CRM dashboard?

48 days overall. Per manager it ranges from 45.8 days (Rocco Neubert) to 49.4 days (Dustin Brinkmann).

Is the data in this CRM dashboard from a real company?

No. It is a sample CRM dataset used to teach live dashboard building in a data analytics bootcamp. The numbers show what the dashboard can surface, not a company's results.

## Air Quality of Dhaka

URL: https://niloy.tech/projects/air-quality/

Dhaka is one of the most polluted cities in the world, and it is where I live. This Data Studio (formerly Looker Studio) dashboard was made for awareness: it charts Dhaka's air quality from AirNow data for January 1, 2023 to January 31, 2024. It shows a peak AQI of 598 on February 18, 2023, counts of days in each AQI category (133 Unhealthy, 101 Very Unhealthy, 14 Hazardous), and breakdowns by hour of day, month and season.

Google Sheets

Data Studio

View live dashboard in Data Studio

Key facts

Data source AirNow.gov, as stated on the dashboard

Time window January 1, 2023 to January 31, 2024 (396 days)

Metrics US AQI and raw PM2.5 concentration, per the dashboard's intro text

Peak and low Highest AQI 598 on February 18, 2023 at 2:00 AM; lowest 18 on November 16, 2023 at 7:00 PM

Granularity Hourly readings from every Dhaka location on AirNow, averaged into daily values

Stack Google Sheets for the calculations, Data Studio for the dashboard

Data

The source is AirNow.gov, the US government's air quality index site, which publishes readings for Dhaka including the US Embassy monitor. Hourly readings from all Dhaka locations available on AirNow for the window were downloaded into Google Sheets.

The US AQI categories, as defined by AirNow: Good 0 to 50, Moderate 51 to 100, Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups 101 to 150, Unhealthy 151 to 200, Very Unhealthy 201 to 300, and Hazardous 301 and higher.

Approach

Daily values. Each day's AQI is the average of its hourly readings.

Calculations in Google Sheets. Days per AQI category, the peak and lowest readings, and the averages by hour of day, month and season are computed in the sheet.

Dashboard. The sheet connects directly to Data Studio as the data source, so the charts read the calculated tables as they are.

What the dashboard shows

Peak and low. The highest AQI recorded in the window is 598, on February 18, 2023 at 2:00 AM, which is in the Hazardous category. The lowest is 18, on November 16, 2023 at 7:00 PM. A line chart plots average, maximum and minimum AQI across the window, with the highest spikes in January to April 2023, the lowest stretch mid-year and a rise again toward December and January.

Days per category. The treemap counts 133 Unhealthy days, 101 Very Unhealthy days, 50 Moderate days and 14 Hazardous days. Those four tiles cover 298 of the 396 days, and no Good tile appears.

By hour. Average AQI is highest at midnight and 1 AM (195) and lowest at 4 PM (147). It falls through the morning, bottoms out in the late afternoon and climbs through the evening.

By month. Average AQI peaks in January (269) and bottoms out in July (94). December (227) and February (225) are next highest after January. The monthly bars aggregate the whole window, so January blends 2023 and 2024.

Seasons. The dashboard describes a winter spike from December to January, relief during the monsoon from June to August, and a rise again from September to November. The month values above follow that pattern.

World comparison. A world map colors countries by AQI on a scale from 4.3 to 229.2.

The dashboard also gives reasons for the night-time peak (temperature inversions and reduced vertical mixing, continuous emissions, flat terrain, calm winds and high humidity) and for the seasonal pattern (rain washing out pollutants in the monsoon, construction and festive activity in autumn). These are explanatory notes on the dashboard, not measurements from the data.

Questions

What was the highest AQI recorded in Dhaka in 2023?

In the AirNow data behind this dashboard, the highest reading is an AQI of 598 on February 18, 2023 at 2:00 AM. Any reading above 300 is in the Hazardous category.

Which month has the worst air quality in Dhaka?

January has the highest average AQI in the dashboard window at 269, followed by December and February. July is the lowest at 94. The window runs from January 2023 to January 2024, so the January figure combines two Januaries.

What time of day is Dhaka's air most polluted?

Averaged over the window, AQI is highest around midnight and 1 AM at 195 and lowest at 4 PM at 147. The dashboard attributes the night-time peak to temperature inversions and continuous emissions.
